personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Dudley is established across multiple volumes with a consistent and layered behavioral profile. He is spoiled, entitled, and physically intimidating, but also cowardly when magic is involved. His dominant mode is aggressive confidence around peers and family who enable him, and panicked retreat when confronted with anything supernatural. He performs emotions strategically — the famous birthday tantrum (Scene 36: 'he wasn't really crying... but he knew that if he screwed up his face and wailed, his mother would give him anything') exemplifies calculated manipulation rather than genuine feeling. His speech is characterized by short, blunt commands ('Make it move,' 'Pass the frying pan,' 'I want to read that letter') and taunts ('Today's your birthday. And nobody cares,' 'Don't kill Cedric! Who's Cedric, your boyfriend?'). He is not stupid in a simple way — he can read situations, and by Book 5 he has developed a genuine physical menace (junior boxing champion). Crucially, he is not a cartoon villain: the books show him to be a product of appalling parenting, capable of rudimentary empathy by Book 7 when he expresses, with agonizing difficulty, that he does not think Harry is a waste of space and acknowledges Harry saved his life.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Dudley's surface traits accurately: the overweight, blond, aggressive bully who manipulates his parents. The birthday present counting scene (Film Scene 2: '36?! But last year, last year I had 37!!') faithfully reproduces the book's entitlement. His cowardice around magic is shown effectively in the Hagrid scene (Film Scene 7: 'I'm-I'm not Harry'). The dementor encounter in Film Scene 14 retains his taunting voice well ('Don't kill Cedric! Who's Cedric, your boyfriend?') and his terror during the dementor attack is shown. His physical presence as a bully is noted. However, the films lose important texture: the calculating fake-crying is absent (replaced by simple bratty complaining), his evolving menace as a boxer is not established, his strategic intelligence in manipulating situations is not demonstrated, and his speech loses the patterned short-command rhythm that marks him in the books. The films reduce him to a reliable sight gag and threat prop.
personality_voice.difference: The core personality type — entitled, cowardly, bullying — is preserved. What is lost is the layering: the deliberate emotional manipulation (fake crying established explicitly in the books), the trajectory from fat child bully to genuinely formidable teenage boxer, and the subtle intelligence that makes him something more than a cartoon bully. The books also give him memorable, rhythmically distinctive taunting dialogue (the Dementor exchange in Book 5 being the most complex — 'I heard you last night, talking in your sleep. Moaning.') which the films approximate but compress. His voice in Film Scene 14 retains the cruelty but loses the sustained cat-and-mouse rhythm of the alleyway confrontation.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The character remains clearly recognizable as Dudley, and the main traits are intact. However, important secondary traits — the deliberate emotional manipulation, the arc of physical menace, and the speech texture — are reduced or absent. This places him in the 14–17 range: recognizable but with noticeable loss of important traits. A score of 17 reflects that the core is faithfully rendered even if the textural layers are missing.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dudley serves multiple narrative functions across the books. (1) He is Harry's primary domestic antagonist and the embodiment of Muggle cruelty and enabled entitlement, which contextualizes why Hogwarts is a liberation. (2) He is a plot driver: his reaction to Harry's Hogwarts letter (Scene 83: 'Dad! Dad, Harry's got a letter!') and his fight for the letter are active narrative contributions. (3) In Book 5, he functions as Harry's first civilian victim of a Dementor attack, which directly triggers the Ministry hearing and the Order's response — a major plot pivot. (4) In Book 7, his goodbye scene is the culmination of a years-long secondary arc about whether any Dursley is capable of humanity; his question 'Why isn't he coming with us?' and his final handshake are narrative acts that force acknowledgment of Harry's worth even from his abuser.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the theatrical films, Dudley retains function (1) clearly. He participates in function (2) at a reduced level (he notices Harry's letter, Film Scene 4, but the fight for it is compressed and his role is brief). His role in function (3) — the dementor attack — is preserved as a plot trigger in Film Scene 14. However, function (4) — the farewell scene — is explicitly excluded from theatrical scoring per the non-theatrical material note; the 'Dudley's goodbye' scene was cut. This removes his most significant narrative act of agency entirely from the theatrical film.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The loss of the farewell scene (cut from theatrical release) is the most significant agency loss. In the books, Dudley's choice to ask about Harry, acknowledge being saved, and offer a handshake is an active narrative moment that closes a character arc and morally functions as a small counterpoint to the Dursleys' cruelty. In the theatrical film, Dudley simply departs with his parents. His role in the dementor plot is retained but his agency within that scene is reduced — he is largely a passive victim rather than someone whose terror and subsequent testimony (at the kitchen table, Scene 473–484) drives the scene's conflict. His letter-spotting moment is retained but brief.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The dementor plot function is preserved, which keeps him from a very low score here. But the loss of the farewell's agency, and the compression of his active role in the letter scenes and post-dementor kitchen confrontation, represent a meaningful reduction. He is still functional as a domestic antagonist, but his capacity to initiate, confront, or change narrative direction is substantially reduced compared to the books. Score of 13 reflects clear alteration of role and agency while acknowledging the dementor pivot is intact.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dudley's motivations in the books are clear if shallow for most of the series: he wants maximum material comfort, peer dominance, and parental validation. He bullies because he can, because it is rewarded, and because Harry's existence is an affront to his status. The more interesting motivational layer emerges in Book 5 and 7: the dementor encounter forces him to confront something real — his own worst memories — and the books explicitly raise the question of what a pampered bully's worst memories actually are (Scene 478: 'What would spoiled, pampered, bullying Dudley have been forced to hear?'). His Book 7 behavior suggests that the dementor experience created genuine internal conflict between his conditioned contempt for Harry and some nascent awareness of Harry's humanity and the reality of danger.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films establish Dudley's surface motivations (entitlement, bullying) effectively. The dementor scene in Film Scene 14 shows his terror, but the film does not develop or explore what memories the dementor surfaced. The post-dementor kitchen scene (Book scenes 473–484) where Dudley slowly, haltingly describes what he experienced ('All went dark. And then I h-heard... things. Inside m-my head.') is present in abbreviated form in the theatrical film — Vernon asks what happened, Dudley responds minimally. The internal conflict this implies — the dawning awareness of genuine darkness beyond his comfortable world — is shown only superficially. The theatrical cut of the farewell scene removes the culmination of any motivational evolution entirely.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The films show the dementor's effect on Dudley but do not develop what this does to him internally. The book's careful attention to what Dudley might have worst memories about (Scene 478) is entirely absent. The motivational evolution from unthinking bully to someone capable of expressing gratitude is lost in the theatrical cut. What remains is the stimulus (dementor attack) without the response arc (changed behavior, gratitude).
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The surface motivations are intact, but the deeper motivational layer — the internal conflict generated by the dementor encounter — is partially shown but not developed, and its culmination is cut. This is a partial alteration and flattening, placing the score in the 8–10 range. Score of 9 reflects that some motivational texture survives but the internal conflict is underexplained to the point of changing the characterization.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for surface; reasonably inferred for internal conflict loss

character_arc.book_baseline: Dudley has a clear arc across the seven books, even if it is a minor one. Starting point: a five-year-old spoiled child whose parents worship him (Book 1). Midpoint development: an increasingly physically menacing teenage bully enabled by his parents, who begins to realize Harry has genuine power over him (Books 2–4). Turning point: the dementor attack in Book 5, which is the first time Dudley is confronted with real consequences — not punishment from adults, but genuine existential horror. His halting description of what he heard/felt (Scenes 476–484) suggests genuine psychic exposure. Resolution: the farewell in Book 7, where Dudley — against everything his upbringing has made him — asks about Harry, acknowledges being saved, says he doesn't think Harry is a waste of space, and shakes his hand. This is not a transformation into a good person, but it is a genuine, hard-won, minimal act of recognition that closes the arc meaningfully.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films show the early-period Dudley (Books 1–2) with reasonable fidelity. The dementor encounter is shown in Film Scene 14. However, the arc's culminating moment — the farewell — is cut from the theatrical release per the non-theatrical material note. Without that scene, there is no resolution to any arc. The dementor attack appears as an isolated event rather than a turning point with consequences. Dudley simply disappears from the films after Book 5 without any acknowledgment of change.
character_arc.difference: The arc's starting and middle points are present. The turning point (dementor encounter) is present but underplayed as an arc moment rather than a catalyst. The resolution — the only moment in which Dudley's arc achieves any kind of completion — is entirely absent from the theatrical release. This means the arc exists in setup but has no payoff.
character_arc.penalty_logic: An arc that is set up but has its resolution entirely removed is significantly altered. The books' arc has a clear, meaningful, emotionally earned endpoint; the theatrical films have none. The dementor encounter loses its narrative weight as a turning point when it has no visible consequence. This is a 'significantly altered' arc per the scoring rubric, placing it in the 5–7 range. Score of 5 reflects that the resolution is not merely compressed but absent.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Dudley's most important relationships: (1) With Harry — a relationship of sustained cruelty and power imbalance that is the defining context of Harry's Muggle life, with a final, fragile pivot to acknowledgment in Book 7. (2) With Vernon and Petunia — a relationship of total indulgence and enabling that explains his character: he is the product of parenting that has never said no. (3) With his gang (Piers, Malcolm, Gordon, etc.) — he is a leader who relies on numbers, which speaks to his cowardice; he needs the gang to feel powerful. The Harry relationship is the most dramatically important, and its arc from bully/victim to an awkward, minimal recognition is irreplaceable. The parental relationship functions as both comedic and explanatory — every scene of Petunia calling him 'Ickle Dudleykins' or Uncle Vernon saying 'Little tyke' contextualizes who Dudley is and why.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Dudley dynamic of cruelty and power imbalance is preserved through Books 1–2 film adaptations (birthday, zoo, letters, dementor). The parental enabling relationship is shown clearly in Film Scenes 2–7, particularly in Petunia's coddling and Vernon's pride. The dementor scene preserves the physical dynamic. However, the final pivot in the Harry-Dudley relationship — the only moment in which the dynamic meaningfully changes — is cut. The gang relationship is mostly absent from the films (Piers appears briefly in Film Scene 3 but the gang dynamic is not developed). The Harry-Dudley relationship therefore ends, in the theatrical film, in its default state of mutual hostility and fear, without any acknowledgment of the arc.
key_relationships.difference: The dominant dynamic of the Harry-Dudley relationship is preserved through the bulk of the story. The loss of the farewell scene means the relationship ends without the pivot that makes it meaningful in retrospect. The gang relationship, which in the books contextualizes Dudley's cowardice (he only attacks with backup), is mostly absent.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The main dynamic is preserved but the emotional endpoint is removed, and a secondary relationship (the gang) is absent. The relationship is mostly faithful through most of the story but loses its most important moment of change. Score of 6 reflects important relationship dynamics that are altered at their culmination and weakened overall.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Dudley in the books is richer than a simple bully. The books include: (1) His deliberate emotional performance — the fake crying is explicitly noted as calculated (Scene 36). (2) The tantrums over food during his diet, where his parents navigate around him, which is both comic and revealing about family dysfunction. (3) The alleyway confrontation in Book 5 (Scenes 393–431), where Dudley gets under Harry's skin by taunting him about Cedric — showing he is perceptive enough to identify Harry's real vulnerabilities. (4) His snoring as a recurring background detail that anchors him as a physical presence in Harry's domestic world. (5) Harry's specific contempt and occasional dark amusement at Dudley (Scene 282: 'He suppressed a laugh as he imagined the look that would spread over Dudley's piggy face'). (6) The diet subplot in Book 4, which is both funny and a study in how the Dursleys respond to any external constraint with denial. (7) Dumbledore's observation in Book 6 (Scene 538) that Dudley has been 'appallingly' damaged by his parents' treatment — which reframes Dudley as a victim of his own upbringing, not merely a perpetrator.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films retain the surface humor (birthday presents, zoo, letters) and the dementor threat. Lost: the fake-crying detail, the diet subplot and its comedy, the alleyway confrontation's full psychological texture (the Cedric taunting and Harry's near-violent response), Dumbledore's observation about Dudley as a victim of his parents, and the farewell scene's humanizing moment. The films also lose the recurring small details that build texture — the snoring, the PlayStation, the five chins, the deliberate descriptions of his size and appetites that make him vivid.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films give Dudley his signature scenes — birthday, zoo, letters, pig tail, dementor — and he is recognizable and often funny. But he functions primarily as a reliable antagonist and comedic target rather than a character with internal contradiction. The nuance that he is both a bully and a damaged child, that his cruelty is enabled by pathological parenting, and that he is capable of a minimal form of moral growth, is almost entirely absent from the theatrical release.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The films preserve the character's broad identity and some of his most memorable moments, but remove most of what gives him complexity: the arc resolution, the psychological texture of the alleyway scene, the reframing via Dumbledore, and the farewell. What remains is a flattened version of Dudley that works as comic relief and a threat but not as a character with internal life. This is major flattening, placing the score in the 5–7 range. Score of 7 reflects that the core is recognizable but the complexity is largely missing.

score_caps_applied: Cap 5 (score above 60 if motivations or arc become unclear, incoherent, or substantially different): Applied. The character arc has no theatrical resolution and motivational evolution is cut, keeping the total at or below 60.

Cap 4 (score above 70 if films preserve only broad identity but remove most of what defines book characterization): Applied as a cross-check — the theatrical films preserve broad identity but remove arc resolution, complexity, and most nuanced material.
comparative.key_observations: Dudley Dursley's theatrical film portrayal is recognizable and faithful in its broad strokes — the spoiled, cowardly, physically imposing bully whose parents enable everything is clearly present across the franchise. The surface humor and the key set-pieces (birthday presents, zoo, letters, pig tail, Dementor attack) are all retained. However, the films systematically lose the layers that make Dudley a character rather than a type: his deliberately calculated emotional manipulation, his arc from child bully to something approaching human recognition, and above all the farewell scene that closes his story. The theatrical cut of 'Dudley's goodbye' is the single most damaging adaptation decision for this character, as it removes the only moment of arc resolution and leaves his relationship with Harry ending in its default state of mutual hostility. The alleyway confrontation in Book 5, though partially present, loses its psychological texture. Dumbledore's reframing of Dudley as a victim of his own upbringing is entirely absent. What survives is a functional comedic antagonist who generates laughs and threat as needed, but not the minor-arc character that Rowling constructed across seven books.
